Here’s a suggested “complete‐SMPS” toolchain built around ON Semiconductor’s own design tools.  We pick one key complementary tool (LTspice) and then show you how it fits into a full workflow, plus some other items you’ll want to have in your toolbox.

1. Recommended Complementary Tool  
   • Tool: LTspice (Linear Technology’s free SPICE simulator)  
   • Why:  
     – Mature, very fast at switching‐converter simulations  
     – Huge device library (including many ON Semi parts)  
     – Built-in waveform viewer, parameter sweeps, Monte Carlo  
     – Zero cost  

2. Strengths & Limitations of LTspice  
   Strengths:  
     • Quick steady-state and transient SMPS switching waveforms  
     • Easy import of manufacturer macromodels (MOSFETs, controllers, diodes)  
     • Good convergence and large community support  
   Limitations:  
     • No native block-diagram control‐system modeling (you can import behavioral sources but it’s clunky)  
     • Limited 3D-EM or thermal co-simulation (just thermal‐resistor models)  
     • Windows-only GUI (there are unofficial workarounds on Linux/Mac)  

3. Complete Workflow & Complementary Tools  
   1) System Specification & Topology Selection  
      – ON Semiconductor design tools (topology advisor, efficiency tables, device selector)  
      – Output: block‐diagram, key specs (Vin, Vout, Iout, switching frequency)  
   2) Circuit‐Level Simulation  
      – LTspice for detailed switching‐waveforms and component stress  
      – Optional: PLECS or MATLAB/Simulink with Simscape Power Systems for mixed analog/digital control loops  
   3) Magnetics Design  
      – Manufacturer’s magnetic-design software (e.g., Würth WE-Magnetics, Magnetics Designer from Coilcraft/Fair-Rite)  
      – Output: core selection, turns, air-gap, copper losses  
   4) Control-Loop/State-Space Modeling  
      – MATLAB/Simulink (Control System Toolbox) or PLECS-Blockset  
      – Output: small-signal model, component values for compensation network  
   5) PCB Layout  
      – Altium Designer (commercial) or KiCad (open source)  
      – Include careful placement of gate drivers, loops, high-di/dt paths  
   6) Thermal & EMI/EMC Analysis  
      – ANSYS Icepak or FloTHERM for 3D thermal simulation  
      – Keysight EMPro or CST Studio for near-field EMI hotspots  
   7) Prototyping & Lab Validation  
      – High-bandwidth oscilloscope (≥200 MHz), differential probes  
      – LCR meter, power analyzer, programmable DC source  
   8) Compliance & Documentation  
      – EMI pre-compliance kit (near-field probes, TEM cell)  
      – Safety test procedures (UL/IEC guidelines)  
      – BOM/cost management (Excel, Altium Vault or Arena PLM)  

4. Practical Tips  
   – Always import the exact ON Semi SPICE macromodel for MOSFETs and controllers rather than using generic parts.  
   – Start with a worst-case thermal‐resistor model in LTspice, but verify with a 3D CFD/thermal tool once you have your board outline.  
   – Keep power loops as small as possible in your PCB layout; simulate parasitic inductances in LTspice by adding small L’s in series.  
   – Do a quick “stability sniff” in the lab: inject a small swept-sine into your feedback network and look for gain/phase margins before full load testing.  
   – Automate your BOM exports from your CAD tool into your purchasing system to avoid part-number mismatches late in the game.  

By combining ON Semiconductor’s topology and device-selection tools with LTspice for waveforms, a block-diagram tool for loop design, dedicated magnetics software, PCB-layout, and then thermal/EMI analysis, you’ll cover every phase of an SMPS design from concept to compliance.

Here’s a breakdown of how ON Semiconductor’s design‐assist suite fits into a broader SMPS workflow, the gaps you’ll typically encounter, and the complementary tools you’ll want to fill them.  

1. What ON Semiconductor Tools Give You—and Where You’ll Need More  
   • Topology selection & device/IC recommendation  
   • Preliminary schematic capture & parametric performance estimates  
   • Basic loss/efficiency curves and output filter guidance  
   Limitations you’ll hit:  
     – No deep-dive SPICE transient or small-signal AC analysis  
     – No magnetics design beyond rough inductor core selection  
     – Limited thermal or EMC/EMI co-simulation  
     – No PCB layout, routing or post-layout extraction  

2. Key Complementary Tools  
   1. SPICE-Level Simulation: LTspice or PSpice  
      – Why?  Industry standard for detailed steady-state, transient and small-signal analysis.  
      – Strengths: free (LTspice); huge device library; scripting for parametric sweeps.  
      – Limitations: no built-in magnetics-winding optimizer; manual subcircuit creation.  
   2. Magnetics Designer: TI Magnetics Designer or Coilcraft’s Toolbox  
      – Why?  Proper inductor/transformer design (winding arrangement, core losses, thermal).  
      – Strengths: core database; automated winding turns and gap calculation; loss modeling.  
      – Limitations: limited topology-aware integration; you must manually import into SPICE.  
   3. System-Level & Real-Time Simulation: PLECS or MathWorks Simulink + Simscape Electrical  
      – Why?  Evaluate interactions among control loops, magnetics, plant models in time domain.  
      – Strengths: block-diagram ease, real-time hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) capability.  
      – Limitations: license cost; steeper learning curve than pure SPICE.  
   4. PCB Layout & Signal Integrity: Altium Designer, Cadence Allegro or KiCad + Mentor HyperLynx  
      – Why?  Proper power-plane stackup, trace impedance, loop-area minimization, decoupling placement.  
      – Strengths: high-end SI/PI/EMI rule checks; 3D clearance; auto-placement aids.  
      – Limitations: cost (Altium/Allegro); KiCad is free but fewer advanced DRC checks.  
   5. Thermal and 3D Field Simulation: ANSYS Icepak/Fluent or COMSOL Multiphysics  
      – Why?  Predict junction, component-level and enclosure thermal behavior; airflow design.  
      – Strengths: full CFD/thermal coupling; power dissipation mapping.  
      – Limitations: long solve times; expensive licenses.  
   6. EMI/EMC Pre-Compliance: Keysight ADS or CST Studio Suite  
      – Why?  Early crosstalk, radiated emission and susceptibility analysis.  
      – Strengths: full-wave solvers; board-level EMI prediction.  
      – Limitations: complexity and licensing cost.  
   7. BOM, Library & Collaboration: Octopart, Upverter, or Altium 365  
      – Why?  Part sourcing, lifecycle status, cost tracking and version-controlled schematics/PCBs.  
      – Strengths: real‐time price/availability; cloud collaboration.  
      – Limitations: integration effort; potential subscription fees.  

3. Example End-to-End Workflow  
   1. Requirements & Topology Selection  
      – Use ON Semi tools to choose buck/boost/flyback/SEPIC and candidate controllers.  
   2. Preliminary Design & Spice Model Setup  
      – Pull ON’s SPICE subcircuits into LTspice or PSpice. Verify switching waveforms and control-loop stability.  
   3. Magnetics Design  
      – Export DC current, ripple specs to TI Magnetics Designer or Coilcraft tool to size cores and windings.  
   4. System-Level Simulation  
      – Rebuild block-diagram in PLECS or Simulink; include magnetics loss models, compensator, and control delays.  
   5. PCB Layout & SI Checks  
      – Layout in Altium or KiCad; use HyperLynx for power-plane impedance and high-di/dt loop checks.  
   6. Thermal & EMI Analysis  
      – Import PCB + component dissipation into Icepak or Fluent for airflow and heatsink sizing.  
      – Do a quick ADS/CST pre-compliance run to locate problem nets.  
   7. Prototype, Lab Validation & Iteration  
      – Build eval board; measure switching waveforms, thermal rise, EMI pre-scan; refine design in tools.  
   8. BOM Finalization & Documentation  
      – Pull final part numbers into Octopart or Altium 365; freeze library; generate fabrication outputs.  

4. Practical Tips  
   – Keep your SPICE and magnetics tool libraries in sync: mismatch in core loss curves or transformer leakage kills performance.  
   – Do your loop-gain AC analysis early—don’t discover subharmonic oscillation on hardware.  
   – Early SI/EMI checks on the PCB reduce board spins. Even a basic 2-layer stackup in KiCad plus HyperLynx go/no-go reports can save weeks.  
   – Automate data hand-off (CSV or XML) between tools when possible. Manual retyping invites errors.  
   – If budget is tight, start with free tools (LTspice, KiCad, TI Magnetics) and graduate to paid solutions as complexity demands.  

By layering these specialized tools on top of ON Semiconductor’s design-assist environment, you’ll cover every stage—from device selection through prototype validation—without gaps in simulation fidelity, manufacturability checks, or compliance readiness.

Here’s a high-level view of how you can stitch a full SMPS/converter workflow around your ON Semiconductor design tools (Webench, design kits, GaN/Si-based reference designs, SPICE models, etc.) and what other tools you’ll want to bring in at each stage.  

1. Schematic Capture & Circuit Simulation  
   – Recommended tool: LTspice (free, widely-used SPICE simulator)  
     • Why: Fast DC/switching/transient analysis, native support for ON Semicon SPICE models, active user community, scripting.  
     • Strengths: Very stable, fast convergence, virtually zero cost, huge library of third-party models.  
     • Limitations: Primitive GUI by today’s standards, limited support for mixed-signal (ideal digital blocks only), no PCB-level parasitic extraction.  

2. Control-Loop & System-Level Modeling  
   – Recommended tool: PLECS Standalone or PLECS Blockset for MATLAB/Simulink  
     • Why: Ideal for power-electronics control loops, seamless integration of PWM, dead-time, saturable magnetics, fast convergence using ideal switch models.  
     • Strengths: Rapid system-level prototyping, auto code generation for DSP/FPGA, built-in magnetic loss and capacitor ESR models.  
     • Limitations: Commercial license required, steeper learning curve if you don’t already use Simulink.  

3. Magnetics Design & Winding Optimization  
   – Recommended tool: FEMM (open-source finite-element magnetics) or Flux (Altair)  
     • Why: Calculate core loss, winding temperature rise, air-gap optimization.  
     • Strengths: Detailed field analysis, accurate loss prediction, handles custom core materials.  
     • Limitations: FEMM has a less polished GUI and no native multi-coil coupling modules; Flux is expensive.  

4. Thermal & Mechanical Analysis  
   – Recommended tool: ANSYS Icepak or FloTHERM  
     • Why: Compute temperature distribution for power losses from both semis and magnetics, optimize heatsink/fan placement.  
     • Strengths: Detailed CFD, conjugate heat transfer, transient and steady-state studies.  
     • Limitations: High license cost, requires powerful workstation, moderate setup time.  

5. EMI/EMC Pre-Compliance  
   – Recommended tool: Keysight EMPro or ADS with EMIT (or CST Studio)  
     • Why: Simulate PCB-level radiated and conducted emissions, iterate filter placement and component selection.  
     • Strengths: 3D field solvers, SI/PI/EMI analysis in a single package, can import your board layouts.  
     • Limitations: Very expensive, quite a learning curve, heavy computational requirements.  

6. PCB Layout  
   – Recommended tool: Altium Designer (commercial) or KiCad (open source)  
     • Why: You’ll need a modern layout tool with differential-pair, embedded-capacitance plane, and 3D clearance checking.  
     • Strengths (Altium): Integrated library/SCH/3D/MCAD; strong push-net and design-rule system. KiCad is free, active community.  
     • Limitations: Altium license cost; KiCad lacks some advanced automation and hot-swap vendor libraries.  

7. BOM Management & Part Selection  
   – Recommended tool: Octopart or SiliconExpert  
     • Why: Real-time price, availability, lifecycle status, and substitution options.  
     • Strengths: Live supply-chain tracking, parametric search, multi-vendor sourcing.  
     • Limitations: Full-function features often behind paywalls; Octopart’s UI can get sluggish with large BOMs.  

8. Prototyping & Lab Validation  
   – Quick-turn PCB: JLCPCB, PCBWay (cost-effective prototypes with >4 layers and impedance control)  
   – Instruments:  
     • Oscilloscope w/high bandwidth and deep memory (e.g. Tektronix MDO/MSO series)  
     • Power analyzer (e.g. Keysight N6705) for efficiency and dynamic load testing  
     • Spectrum analyzer + LISN for EMI injections  

Practical Tips  
 A. Start your filter/EMI layout early. Carve out space for line-input common-mode chokes, Y-caps and test points.  
 B. Place high-di/dt loops (switch node, Cboot, MOSFET-driver decoupling) as compactly as possible.  
 C. Use thermal vias under power components and a solid copper pour tied to the heatsink.  
 D. Validate your control-loop margins with both simulation (Bode plots in PLECS/MATLAB) and hardware (gain/phase injection).  
 E. Automate your BOM checks weekly to catch parts at risk of obsolescence.  

Example Workflow Summary  
 1. ON Semi Webench → generate initial topology, parts list, and SPICE deck  
 2. LTspice → verify DC-DC transients, switch-node waveforms, steady-state losses  
 3. PLECS → model full system including control loop, check start-up, transient response  
 4. FEMM/Flux → finalize magnetics geometry and loss estimates  
 5. Icepak/FloTHERM → thermal check under worst-case loading  
 6. ADS/EMPro → pre-compliance EMI assessment, iterate on input/output filters  
 7. Altium/KiCad → detailed PCB layout, design-rule and impedance check  
 8. Octopart → firm up the BOM and purchase orders  
 9. JLCPCB/PCBWay → order prototypes; debug in the lab with scope, power analyzer, spectrum analyzer  
10. Revise layout/schematics based on lab findings, update simulation models, repeat as needed  

Bringing these tools together will give you a robust, end-to-end SMPS / converter design flow that complements ON Semiconductor’s platform, minimizes surprises in the lab, and smooths your path from initial concept to production.

Below is a side-by-side look at ON Semiconductor’s design suite versus Analog Devices’ ADIsimPower for a 12 V → 3.3 V buck converter, followed by my recommendation, their respective strengths/limitations, a suggested workflow (including complementary tools), and some hands-on tips.  

1. Comparison Summary  
   • ON Semiconductor Design Tools  
     – Web-based buck-converter configurator + downloadable GUI tool (“GreenPAK Designer” for logic/PWM, “FET Selection Tool,” etc.)  
     – Pre-validated reference designs (schematics, PCB layouts, thermal models) for ON’s MOSFETs, controllers, inductors  
     – Integrated thermal & efficiency plots, worst-case tolerance sweeps  
     – Automatic BOM generator pulling live ON part data & pricing  
   • ADIsimPower  
     – Windows GUI plus Excel-based toolkits (or online) supporting ADI’s regulators, dc-dc, LDOs  
     – Spice-level simulation of switching waveforms, loop-stability analysis (Bode plots), transient responses  
     – Easy param sweep of external components (inductor, cap, catch diode)  
     – Built-in LTspice export and netlist generation for detailed simulation  

2. Recommended Tool  
   For a green-field 12 V → 3.3 V design, I recommend ADIsimPower if your goal is deep loop stability analysis and multi-vendor component­-level simulation. If you plan to stay exclusively on ON Semiconductor parts and want turnkey reference-design layouts + vendor-locked BOM, the ON tool streamlines that process.  

3. Strengths and Limitations  
   ON Semiconductor Design Tools  
     Strengths:  
       • Immediate access to ON’s latest power MOSFETs, drivers, controllers, inductors, capacitors with vendor-tested configs  
       • Built-in PCB layouts and thermal models reduce your front-end effort  
       • Single-click BOM with live pricing & lead-time visibility  
     Limitations:  
       • Less granular Spice-level control of loop‐gain / compensation networks  
       • Can’t easily swap in 3rd-party inductors or capacitors beyond ON’s catalog  
   ADIsimPower  
     Strengths:  
       • Spice-grade waveforms, Bode-plot tweaking of compensation network, transient start-up inrush analysis  
       • Flexibility to choose any vendor’s magnetics, diodes, caps  
       • Export to LTspice / PSpice for extended EM/RF analysis or resonance modeling  
     Limitations:  
       • You need to assemble your own BOM and live-time procurement data  
       • Fewer turnkey PCB layouts—layout guidelines only, not full Gerbers  

4. Suggested Workflow with Complementary Tools  
   a. Top-Level Specs & Part Shortlist  
     • Use your chosen tool (ADIsimPower or ON’s configurator) to set VIN=12 V, VOUT=3.3 V, IOUT_max, switching frequency, efficiency vs. thermal trade-off.  
   b. Preliminary Simulation & Compensation  
     • If using ADIsimPower: generate Bode plots, transient start-up waveforms, output-step response.  
     • If using ON’s tool: verify empirical efficiency/thermal curves; note recommended compensation components.  
   c. Detailed Spice Modeling  
     • Export netlist to LTspice or PSpice.  
     • Layer in parasitics (layout inductance, ESR/ESL of caps, diode recovery).  
   d. Thermal & Layout Validation  
     • Import PCB outlines into a 2D/3D field solver (e.g. ANSYS SIwave, Cadence Sigrity, or free QuCS Studio for quick checks).  
     • Use a thermal sim (e.g. Mentor HyperLynx or SolidWorks Flow Simulation) to validate hotspot temps.  
   e. Gerber & BOM Finalization  
     • For an ON-based design: grab the reference-design Gerbers and adapt for your board stack-up.  
     • For ADI-based or hybrid: build your BOM in a tool like Altium Concord Pro or BOM DFM software to lock in live vendor pricing & alternate sources.  
   f. Prototyping & Lab Characterization  
     • Bring-up on a bench supply, scope, thermal camera.  
     • Verify line/load regulation, transient recovery, EMI pre-compliance with a near-field probe.  

5. Practical Tips  
   • Compensation margins: Always verify phase margin (≥45°) and gain margin (≥10 dB) under worst-case min-VIN, max-load, cold start.  
   • Layout first: Switch nodes and power loops should be minimized; use a polygon pour for the inductor ground return. Build your board outline early and then port your schematic to match it.  
   • Thermal headroom: Use a 4-layer board or a thick copper pour under the MOSFET to keep junction ≤ 100 °C at full load.  
   • BOM alternates: Component lead times shift rapidly. Lock in second‐source inductors and caps early.  
   • EMI filtering: Add a small RC snubber or feed-through bead on the output if you see high-frequency spikes.  

Bottom line:  
– If you want a fast, ON-parts-only path with reference layouts and turnkey BOM generation, stick with ON Semiconductor Design Tools.  
– If you need deep loop analysis, cross-vendor flexibility, and Spice export for advanced sims, go with ADIsimPower.

Below is a side-by-side comparison of ON Semiconductor’s Design Tools vs. ADIsimPower for a 12 V→3.3 V buck-converter project, a recommendation on which to lean toward, plus a suggested workflow and some hands-on tips.

1. Recommended Primary Tool  
   ON Semiconductor Design Tools  
   • Why:  
     – Tailored for ON Semi power MOSFETs, controllers and integrated converters.  
     – Fully integrated web-based GUI for part selection, parametric searches, schematic capture and PSpice-based time-domain waveforms.  
     – Instant BOM exports, PCB-footprint references and thermal / efficiency estimates.  
     – No additional install if you’re already using ON’s apps; the learning curve is minimal if you’ve targeted ON devices.  

   If your design absolutely requires an ADI regulator or you need fine-tuned compensation-loop optimization built into the tool GUI, then ADIsimPower is your second choice.  

2. Strengths & Limitations  

   ON SEMICONDUCTOR DESIGN TOOLS  
   Strengths  
   • Device‐centric filters let you quickly narrow to synchronous buck controllers (e.g. NCP303xx, NCP163xx series) or power stages (FDMF…) that meet your current/voltage/efficiency targets.  
   • Integrated PSpice models let you “click-to-simulate” your exact part in steady-state and transient modes (start-up, load-step, short-circuit).  
   • BOM, thermal derating curves and PCB‐footprint data all exported from one place.  
   • Free, no-install web portal; up-to-date models.  

   Limitations  
   • Only ON Semiconductor parts are covered.  
   • The GUI is less flexible than a full SPICE IDE; deep loop-compensation wizardry may require manual SPICE tweaking.  

   ADISIMPOWER  
   Strengths  
   • Excellent built-in compensation network designer for ADI’s controllers.  
   • Works with LTspice net-lists so you can leverage custom models or third-party devices.  
   • Rich transient-waveform viewer, parametric sweeps, and Fourier analysis for EMI studies.  

   Limitations  
   • Limited to Analog Devices’ part portfolio.  
   • Standalone Windows application—requires installation and periodic updates.  
   • No direct BOM export or PCB-footprint database.  

3. Workflow & Complementary Tools  

   A. Define Specs  
     1. Input range: 12 V nominal (10–14 V worst-case).  
     2. Output: 3.3 V ±1%, 1–5 A.  
     3. Efficiency target: ≥ 90% at full load.  
     4. Switching frequency: 500 kHz–2 MHz.  
     5. Thermal budget, ripple, EMI constraints.  

   B. Part Selection & Initial Simulation (ON Semiconductor Design Tools)  
     1. Open the Web-Portal “Power Design Tool.”  
     2. Enter your specs; filter for synchronous buck controllers + MOSFETs.  
     3. Review candidate topologies (single-stage vs. controller + external FETs).  
     4. Generate a preliminary schematic and run the built-in PSpice transient sim.  
     5. Check: inrush, load-step response, efficiency curve vs. load.  

   C. Deep-dive SPICE & Loop Compensation  
     1. Export SPICE netlist to PSpice (or LTspice if you prefer).  
     2. Tweak R-C network around the error amplifier for phase/gain margins.  
     3. Run Bode-plot AC sweep, load-step transients, worst-case input.  

   D. Layout & Thermal Analysis  
     1. Export BOM + footprints to your PCB tool (Altium, KiCad, OrCAD).  
     2. Follow the layout guidelines from ON Semi application notes:  
        – Minimize high-di/dt loop.  
        – Place input/output caps close to VIN, SW, and GND pins.  
        – Use a solid copper pour for PGND, connect to AGND at a single point.  
     3. (Optional) Export to a thermal-solver (ANSYS Icepak, FloTHERM) for hotspot checks.  

   E. Prototyping & Validation  
     1. Build a bench prototype.  
     2. Confirm: efficiency curve, output ripple, transient recovery.  
     3. EMI scan—tweak snubbers or ferrite beads if needed.  
     4. Iterate compensation if loop-gain shifts under real-world parasitics.  

4. Practical Tips  

   – Always grab the latest .lib / .mod files from ON’s website before you begin simulating.  
   – When simulating, sweep across worst-case input (10–14 V) and worst-case ambient.  
   – Use a small-signal AC sweep (0 dBm source) at your feedback divider node to verify ≥ 45° phase margin.  
   – Keep MOSFET switching node (SW) trace as short as possible; avoid routing over splits in ground plane.  
   – Deploy low-ESR ceramic caps on the output, plus a small bulk electrolytic to tame mid-band resonances.  
   – If your 12 V rail is “noisy,” add an LC EMI filter up-front—ON’s tool can size that too.  
   – Record real-load waveforms on a 500 MHz scope with >100 MHz probes to capture ringing and overshoot.  

By leaning on ON Semi’s Design Tools as your backbone, you’ll speed up part selection, get built-in SPICE models, and rapidly generate BOM/layout data. If down the road you want to explore an ADI controller or need LTspice-centric compensation wizards, you can slot ADIsimPower in for that phase of the design.

Recommended Tool  
I recommend using ON Semiconductor’s Web-based Design Suite as your primary starting point for a 12 V→3.3 V buck, then validating and fleshing out the design in ADIsimPower (or in a SPICE environment).  Here’s why:  
• ON Semi’s tool is tailor-made for ON’s buck regulators, giving you parts screening, schematic wizards and a first-pass BOM in seconds.  
• ADIsimPower (or its sister tool, LTpowerCAD from ADI) offers deeper loop-compensation guidance, detailed switch-node waveforms, transient and thermal plots, and an integrated SPICE netlist export.  

In short – pick your ON-chip in ON’s tool, then port the parameters and netlist into ADIsimPower (or LTspice) for final tuning and margin checks.  

1. Strengths and Limitations  
1.1 ON Semiconductor Design Tools  
  Strengths:  
  – Instant device selection from ON’s portfolio (buck, boost, synchronous).  
  – Automated schematic capture + BOM export.  
  – Built-in switch-node waveform estimates, thermal pad-loss calculators.  
  – Very low learning curve if you’re targeting ON parts.  
  Limitations:  
  – Limited to ON’s product families.  
  – Compensation guidance is more “rule-of-thumb” (type-II vs type-III) with fewer interactive Bode-plot tools.  
  – No built-in SPICE or detailed transient/EMI analysis.  

1.2 ADIsimPower (or LTpowerCAD)  
  Strengths:  
  – Broad multi-vendor library (ADI, Linear Tech, etc.).  
  – Interactive loop-compensation design: see gain/phase margin, adjust R-C zeros/poles.  
  – Full switching-waveform, transient step-load, thermal-stress plotting.  
  – Exportable SPICE netlist for any SPICE engine (LTspice, PSpice).  
  Limitations:  
  – Slightly steeper learning curve to master the compensation tables.  
  – Doesn’t auto-build your PCB footprints or full parametric BOM (you enter components by hand).  
  – Some parts (very latest ON devices) may lag behind ON’s own library.  

2. High-Level Workflow with Complementary Tools  
Step 1: Part Selection & Preliminary Sizing (ON Semiconductor Design Tool)  
  • Enter Vin=12 V, Vout=3.3 V, Iout_max (e.g. 5 A), switching frequency target (e.g. 500 kHz).  
  • Tool will suggest one or two candidate ON regulators (e.g. NCP3065, NCP3063, NCP5380).  
  • Download the automatic Eagle/Altium/PCB library, schematic snippet, and initial BOM.  

Step 2: Loop Compensation & Transient Analysis (ADIsimPower)  
  • Pick the same topology in ADIsimPower; replicate your inductor, output-cap, Rfb values.  
  • Use the built-in loop-analyzer to verify gain margin (>10 dB) and phase margin (>45°).  
  • Run load-step (0→100% load) and line-step simulations to check overshoot, undershoot, recovery time.  

Step 3: Spice-Level Verification (LTspice or PSpice)  
  • Export netlist from ADIsimPower or rebuild your exact schematic in LTspice.  
  • Inject parasitic ESR/ESL for inductors and caps to capture ringing.  
  • Run switching-node FFT to quantify EMI.  

Step 4: Thermal & PCB Layout Co-Design (ANSYS Icepak, FloTHERM, or Cortex-PLECS)  
  • Import the footprint and power-loss numbers (switching + conduction losses).  
  • Simulate junction temperature at your target ambient and airflow.  
  • Iterate copper pours, thermal vias, heatsink or plane thickness.  

3. Practical Tips  
 • Always cross-check ON’s loss tables against your real-world inductor DCR and actual cap ESR. Manufacturer datasheets sometimes quote “ideal” values.  
 • If you see excessive switch-node ringing in SPICE, add a 2–5 Ω snubber or a small R in series with the gate.  
 • Capacitor derating: use X5R/X7R types at twice the voltage rating (6.3 V or 10 V for 3.3 V rail) to maintain capacitance under bias.  
 • For loop-tweaking, change one compensation component at a time and re-measure gain/phase. Keep a lab notebook or version-control your netlists.  
 • Before prototype spin, build a simple breadboard test with only the power stage and sense lines tied out to an oscilloscope. Validate switch waveform shape and ripple.  
 • Use demonstration boards from ON and ADI as a reference for layout best practices (ground islands, phase-node copper pours, decoupling placement).  

Summary  
 • Start in ON Semiconductor’s design suite to lock in part number, schematic and rough loss estimate.  
 • Port your design into ADIsimPower (or LTpowerCAD) for in-depth loop analysis and SPICE netlist export.  
 • Final-stage verify in a pure SPICE tool (LTspice/PSpice) with parasitics, then move on to thermal layout co-design.  
 • This hybrid approach leverages the strengths of both tools and gives you confidence from schematic to manufactured board.

Here’s how I arrived at the recommendation for a “one-stop” SMPS/converter toolchain and why it will work end-to-end in your project.  

1. Design Goals and Constraints  
   • You need to go from specs (Vin/Vout, power, topology) through component sizing, dynamic behavior, magnetics, PCB layout, BOM and finally bench validation.  
   • You’ll want a mix of vendor-supported modules (to accelerate your first prototype) plus neutral tools for deeper customization and pre-compliance checks.  
   • Cost, learning curve, and integration (i.e. how easily you can move a design from simulation to layout to test) are key decision factors.  

2. Candidate Tools and Trade-Offs  
   ON Semiconductor Power Supply Designer (PSD)  
     Strengths:  
       – Web-based GUI lets you pick topology, fill in specs, and instantly get an ON-semi-optimized BOM and reference schematic.  
       – Tight integration with ON part libraries (great for first prototype).  
     Limitations:  
       – Not meant for nonlinear dynamic behavior beyond steady-state; limited magnetics insight; can’t do EMI/thermal analysis.  
   LTspice (Analog Devices)  
     Strengths:  
       – Free, very mature; huge library of switch-mode parts (including ON-semi) and third-party models.  
       – Fast time-domain switching simulation and parametric sweeps.  
     Limitations:  
       – Limited support for control-loop auto-tuning; magnetics are manual; GUI dated.  
   PLECS (Plexim)  
     Strengths:  
       – Purpose-built for power electronics: ideal-switch models, built-in magnetics blocks, controller auto-tune, temperature.  
       – Seamless transition between block and Spice‐level detail.  
     Limitations:  
       – Paid license; can be overkill for simple buck/boost designs.  
   FEMM (Free finite element magnetics)  
     Strengths:  
       – Free 2D electromagnetic field solver; great for transformer/inductor core/bobbin geometry.  
     Limitations:  
       – No thermal coupling; 3D not supported.  
   Altium Designer / KiCad  
     Strengths Altium: full-featured, automated DRC, rule-driven power layout wizards.  
               KiCad: open-source, zero license cost, decent power-layouts.  
     Limitations:  
       – Altium is expensive; KiCad less polished for high‐speed/EMC.  
   EMI Pre-Compliance Suite (e.g. EMCoS, COMSOL)  
     Strengths: catch radiated/conducted noise early.  
     Limitations: add-on cost, steep learning curve.  

3. How the Pieces Fit Together (Workflow)  
   1. Specification & Topology Definition  
      – Start in ON-Semi Power Supply Designer: enter Vin, Vout, Iout, switching frequency, thermal limits.  
      – Get initial schematic, component list, ferrite core selection, and preliminary PCB footprints.  
   2. Fast-Switching Simulation  
      – Export that schematic to LTspice (ON-semi provides symbols/models).  
      – Run time-domain sweeps, parametric corner-case sims (load step, input step, short-circuit).  
      – Verify steady-state waveforms, losses, ripple.  
   3. Control-Loop & Magnetic Sub-System Tuning  
      – Import converter topology into PLECS for loop-gain analysis and auto-tune of compensation network.  
      – Use PLECS’ magnetic blocks or link to FEMM to validate core losses and winding counts.  
   4. Detailed Magnetics Design  
      – Bring core geometry into FEMM; refine window utilization, ensure flux density limits and thermal hotspots.  
   5. PCB Layout  
      – Move finalized schematic into Altium (or KiCad if cost is a constraint).  
      – Follow power-layout best-practices (short loops, Kelvin grounds, plane stacking, thermal vias).  
      – Run embedded DRC/DRC rules for creepage, clearance, impedance, heat spread.  
   6. EMI/EMC Pre-Check  
      – Use a fast pre-compliance tool or s-parameter solver to locate potential radiators, adjust placement/shielding.  
   7. Prototype & Validation  
      – Order boards/BOM; assemble.  
      – On the bench: scope and power analyzer for efficiency and dynamic tests; spectrum analyzer for EMI.  
      – Iterate: feed data back into LTspice/PLECS to refine component values.  

4. Practical Tips  
   • Keep your BOM anchored in a single database (Altium Vault, Excel + scripting, or an ECAD/PDM system) so cost and availability follow along.  
   • Invest early effort in magnetic parts—an optimized inductor often makes more difference than exotic semiconductors.  
   • Calibrate your models: measure real-world Rds(on), inductance vs. current, and thermal resistance, then update your simulator.  
   • Lay out switching nodes first: high-di/dt loops create most EMI; keep those loops small and planar.  
   • Automate common sweeps: overload, turn-on/off, ambient temperature extremes. A little scripting in LTspice or PLECS saves days.  
   • Build in test points or use mezzanine PCBs so you can probe waveforms without tearing apart the board.

     – If Tj is too high or ΔT across the board is unacceptable, go back to PLECS:  
       • Try a different MOSFET with lower total gate charge or RDS(on).  
       • Re‐optimize magnetics (thicker core, different material, higher winding copper area).  
       • Adjust layout: add thermal vias, thicken copper pours, or increase convection area.  
     – Re‐export and re‐solve until both electrical efficiency (≥ your target) and thermal margins (Tj ≤ 100 °C under worst‐case) are met.  

4. Practical Tips  
   • Always start with the worst‐case: maximum ambient, maximum load, minimum airflow.  
   • Pull manufacturer’s loss curves (Conduction vs. Id, Eoss vs. Vds) and fit them into your PLECS blocks.  
   • In PLECS, use a two‐stage simulation: begin with a coarse step to reach steady‐state quickly, then switch to fine time steps around switching edges to capture losses accurately.  
   • In Icepak/FloTHERM, validate your CFD model by comparing predictions against a small prototype’s measured temperatures (board‐mounted thermocouples).  
   • If you’re cost- or time-sensitive, you can skip full CFD: use PLECS’ thermal network alone (with conservative convection resistor values) to get a first‐cut predictions before committing to 3D CFD.  
   • Keep your toolchain traceable: maintain versioned netlists, thermal‐model parameters and layout exports so you can audit how each change affected both losses and thermal performance.  

By combining ON Semi’s part libraries and topology tools with a fast, loss-aware simulator like PLECS and a detailed CFD/thermal tool like Ansys Icepak, you’ll have a tightly integrated workflow for hitting both your efficiency targets and thermal-management requirements.

2. Built-in thermal‐network elements to represent junction, case, and heatsink thermal resistances and capacitances.

Complementary Workflow  
1. Topology & Component Selection (ON Semi Design Tools, TI WEBENCH, Infineon Designer):  
   – Preliminary power stage topology, preliminary magnetics sizing, switch selection.  
2. Circuit & Loss Simulation (PLECS):

   – Extract steady-state power dissipations for each power semiconductor and magnetics.  
3. PCB Layout & SI/PI Checks (Altium/OrCAD + Ansys SIwave or Cadence Sigrity):

4. Thermal‐Network & 3D-CFD (ANSYS Icepak or FloTHERM):

Practical Tips  
• Use actual loss‐map data for your chosen MOSFETs/IGBTs—don’t rely on generic RDS(on) models.  
• Separate simulation time‐scales: run fast transient SW simulations in PLECS; couple to slower thermal network for junction-to-ambient modeling.  
• In PLECS thermal networks, model both junction-to-case and case-to-heatsink Rθ, and include thermal capacitances for dynamic heating.  
• When exporting to CFD, simplify geometry (remove tiny features) to speed up mesh convergence.  
• Validate simulated junction temps against bench data—use thermocouples mounted on TO-220/TO-247 cases and IR imaging for hotspots.  
• Iterate magnetics design: excessive core or copper losses will raise winding and core temps; feed those losses back into your thermal model.  
• Leverage co-simulation with MATLAB/Simulink if you have control-loop or system-level interactions to capture both control dynamics and power/thermal behaviors.

Recommended Tool: Plexim PLECS Why PLECS?  
PLECS is a purpose-built power-electronics simulation environment that combines fast time-domain switching simulations with built-in loss and thermal modeling. It can handle average‐value and full‐switching models, offers tight integration with MATLAB/Simulink (if you need controls), and produces per-device loss breakdowns automatically.

Strengths  
• Simulation speed: orders of magnitude faster than generic SPICE for PWM converters.  
• Automatic loss calculation: conduction, switching, gate, magnetic core, winding, etc.  
• Thermal network modeling: attach thermal RC elements to power devices to predict junction temperatures.  
• Ease of use: drag-and-drop library of semiconductors, magnetics, passive elements.  
• HIL support: ready for hardware-in-the-loop if you graduate to controller testing.

Limitations  
• 3D mechanical/airflow thermal details are limited—you’ll need a dedicated FEA/CFD tool for complex heatsinks or airflow patterns.  
• Magnetic component design is more “black-box” (you supply loss curves or model parameters rather than detailed geometry).  
• Licensing cost—smaller labs may find it pricier than free SPICE tools.

Complementary Workflow  
1. Initial Topology & Sizing (ON Semiconductor Webench)  
   – Define input/output specs, pick switching topology (buck, boost, flyback, etc.), and get a first cut on component values and expected efficiencies.  

2. Detailed Circuit & Loss Simulation (PLECS)  
   – Model your full converter with real device models from ON Semi (IGBTs, MOSFETs, diodes).  
   – Run steady-state and transient tests.  
   – Extract per-device loss vs. load, temperature, switching frequency.

3. Thermal FEA/CFD (ANSYS Icepak or FloEFD)  
   – Import PCB and heatsink geometry.  
   – Map PLECS-computed losses onto each device footprint.  
   – Simulate conduction, convection, radiation. Optimize heatsink fins, airflow, copper pour.  

4. Layout & Verification (ECAD + Builder)  
   – Implement your refined component placement, copper pours, thermal vias in your ECAD tool (Altium, PADS).  
   – Export for another quick PLECS run or SPICE-level check to verify stray inductances.  

5. Hardware Prototyping & Thermal Validation  
   – Build a lever-arm prototype.  
   – Measure device temperatures with thermocouples/RTDs and IR camera.  
   – Compare to simulation, adjust thermal boundary conditions or heatsink design as needed.

Practical Tips  
• Always validate loss models: compare PLECS’ predicted switching and conduction losses to datasheet curves at your operating voltages/currents.  
• Use a multi-load sweep (light, medium, full) to catch worst-case—islands of high loss at half-load, for example.  
• In thermal FEA, set realistic ambient conditions (incl. board conduction paths) and consider worst-case airflow (e.g. low‐speed forced convection).  
• Implement thermal vias and copper pours under power packages in your PCB layout to reduce θ_J-A (junction-to-ambient) resistance.  
• Build in at least a 20 °C thermal margin between predicted T_J(max) and your rated device T_J(max) to account for model or process variations.  
• Iterate: small changes in switching speed or gate drive levels can greatly affect switching losses (and therefore thermal performance), so loop back to PLECS whenever you adjust key drive parameters.
